sentences.text: Many decisions happen by gathering uncertain information, called noisy evidence, over time until this evidence reaches a set limit, known as a threshold or bound, which then determines the choice and how long it takes to decide.
In perception, the strength of a stimulus, measured by its signal-to-noise ratio, affects how quickly and accurately decisions are made, as well as how confident people feel about those decisions.
The study predicted that increasing noise, or randomness, in the information would cause decisions to be made faster, reduce accuracy, but surprisingly increase confidence.

To test this, researchers developed a new sensory manipulation that adds unbiased noise to motion-selective areas of the visual cortex, and confirmed this effect by recording brain activity from motion-sensitive neurons in macaque monkeys' areas MT and MST.

Both humans and monkeys showed faster decisions and higher confidence when noise was increased, across different stimulus strengths, while their accuracy was only slightly affected and not significantly reduced.

The size of these effects on decision speed and confidence matched the predictions of a bounded evidence accumulation model, which explains decisions as the process of gathering noisy evidence until a threshold is reached.

sentences.text: The deamidase OspI from the bacterium Shigella flexneri changes a specific amino acid, glutamine at position 100, in the human protein UBC13 into glutamate, a process called deamidation.
This chemical change stops UBC13 from working with another protein called TRAF6 to add chains of ubiquitin, which normally helps activate the NF-κB inflammatory response in the immune system.
Deamidation weakens the interaction between UBC13 and the TRAF6 RING domain by disturbing both their stable (native) and temporary (transient) contacts.
The change creates a new electrical bond inside UBC13 that competes with an important bond between UBC13 and TRAF6, reducing how well they stick together.
This competition between bonds also disrupts the temporary interactions needed for UBC13 and RING proteins to form their usual complex.
Additionally, the new negative charge on UBC13 repels the negatively charged surface of the RING domain, making it harder for the proteins to come close and interact.
Overall, this post-translational modification by deamidation changes the shape and stability of temporary protein complexes, reducing their ability to bind and function properly.

sentences.text: Working memory relies on coordinated interactions among large-scale distributed brain networks, especially involving frontal and parietal brain regions.
Oscillatory synchronization, particularly in the theta frequency range (around 4-6 Hz), helps different brain regions communicate during working memory tasks.

In this study, researchers applied theta-frequency (6 Hz) transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) to the right frontoparietal network, targeting the middle frontal gyrus and inferior parietal lobule, to modulate brain activity supporting working memory.

They used synchronous (in-phase) and desynchronous (out-of-phase) tACS while participants performed memory tasks of varying difficulty, including the 2-back task, which requires monitoring and recalling sequences.
Applying synchronous theta-frequency tACS to the right frontoparietal network improved working memory performance when cognitive demands were high, such as during the 2-back task.
Specifically, synchronous tACS led to faster reaction times in the 2-back task compared to desynchronous stimulation and sham conditions.
Brain imaging using fMRI showed that the effects of tACS on brain activity and connectivity depended on the relative phase of the stimulation and the cognitive state during the task.

While synchronous and desynchronous stimulation produced different brain activity and connectivity patterns during the demanding 2-back task, they caused similar activity changes and no connectivity effects during a simpler control task called the Choice Reaction Task (CRT).
During synchronous tACS in the verbal working memory task, activity increased in the parietal cortex, a brain area important for memory, and this increase was linked to better behavioral performance.
The relative timing (phase) of stimulation between frontal and parietal brain areas influenced functional connectivity, changing how these regions communicated during working memory tasks.

Synchronous tACS increased connectivity from the inferior parietal lobule to frontal parts of the frontoparietal network, such as the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, which are important for working memory processing.
Overall, the study found a direct link between better behavioral performance in a demanding working memory task and large-scale brain synchronization across the right frontoparietal network.

sentences.text: The granular retrosplenial cortex (RSG) is a brain area important for both spatial and non-spatial behaviors, but how it processes these different types of information is not well understood.
Researchers used a method called optogenetic circuit mapping, which activates neurons with light, to study how different brain regions connect to specific neuron types in the RSG of mice.

They found that inputs from the anterior thalamus and dorsal subiculum, which carry spatial information, strongly and selectively activate a special type of neuron in the RSG called low-rheobase (LR) pyramidal cells.

In contrast, inputs from the claustrum and anterior cingulate cortex, which mostly carry non-spatial information, preferentially activate neighboring regular-spiking (RS) pyramidal neurons in the RSG.

This separation is possible because the branches of these neurons and the incoming axons are precisely arranged in different sublayers within layer 1 of the RSG, allowing parallel processing of spatial and non-spatial signals.

The way thalamic inputs change over time, called thalamocortical synaptic dynamics, allows LR neurons to calculate the speed of head rotation even though the inputs only provide information about head direction, not speed.
Together, these parallel input streams highlight LR neurons as a distinct type of neuron in the RSG that is well positioned to support computations related to spatial orientation.

sentences.text: Petals help open the flower and attract pollinators, so having a stable number of petals ensures a reliable display of reproductive organs and consistent signals for pollinators.
Arabidopsis thaliana flowers consistently have four petals regardless of genetic differences, showing that petal number is a stable trait in this species.
While Arabidopsis flowers always have four petals, Cardamine hirsuta flowers can have between zero and four petals, showing variable petal number within this species.
Differences in the APETALA1 gene, called AP1, between Arabidopsis thaliana and Cardamine hirsuta explain why Arabidopsis has a stable petal number while Cardamine hirsuta has variable petal number.
The AP1 gene from Arabidopsis thaliana makes petal number stable by hiding the effects of other genes that would cause petal number to vary in Cardamine hirsuta.

The AP1 gene from Cardamine hirsuta cannot replace the function of the Arabidopsis AP1 gene that stabilizes petal number, and differences in the gene’s upstream regulatory regions contribute to this effect.
Even though Cardamine hirsuta has enough genetic variation to produce flowers with four petals, natural populations still show variable petal numbers.

sentences.text: Some viruses, including Marburg virus, Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), and Dengue virus, activate and benefit from the protein Nrf2, which controls gene expression.
Before this study, the effect of activating Nrf2 on HIV infection was unknown.
Sulforaphane (SFN), a compound produced in cruciferous vegetables like broccoli after damage, activates Nrf2 and strongly changes gene expression in cells.
This study found that SFN blocks HIV infection in primary macrophages but does not block infection in primary T cells.

Removing Nrf2 using siRNA increased HIV infection in macrophages and reduced SFN's ability to block the virus; SFN also blocked HIV in PMA-differentiated promonocytic cell lines but not in other tested cell lines.
SFN works by activating Nrf2, which triggers the antiviral effect against HIV infection.

SFN blocks HIV infection after the virus enters macrophages but before the formation of 2-LTR circles, a step needed before viral DNA integrates into the host genome, similar to the antiviral proteins SAMHD1 and MX2.
Unlike some antiviral responses, SFN does not increase levels of the antiviral proteins SAMHD1 or MX2 during HIV inhibition.
This study shows for the first time that activating Nrf2 can strongly block HIV infection, revealing a new way to trigger antiviral activity.

sentences.text: Aedes-borne arboviruses such as dengue and Zika continue to cause epidemics worldwide.
In the Dominican Republic, a large dengue epidemic was quickly followed by Zika virus cases, allowing study of the different transmission drivers between these two flaviviruses.
Researchers used retrospective datasets to collect information on populations at risk and describe dengue, Zika, and Guillain-Barre syndrome outbreaks on a national scale.
Most dengue cases (75%) occurred in people under 20 years old, while Zika infections were more evenly spread across age groups.
Dengue attack rates were slightly higher in males at 25.9 per 10,000 population compared to 21.5 per 10,000 in females.
Zika infections were clustered among females, who made up 73.8% of cases, with age-adjusted attack rates of 7.64 per 10,000 compared to 2.72 per 10,000 in males.
The basic reproduction number (R0) for Zika was higher in females at 1.84 than in males at 1.72, indicating greater transmission potential among females.
Guillain-Barre syndrome attack rates were slightly higher in males (0.62 per 10,000) than females (0.57 per 10,000) during the Zika outbreak.
Existing dengue immunity appeared to have little impact on reported Zika attack rates at the population level in the Dominican Republic.

Community awareness campaigns likely caused increased reporting of Zika among women of reproductive age by influencing short-term health seeking behaviour, though biological susceptibility cannot be excluded.
Media campaigns and screening are recommended for women of reproductive age during Zika outbreaks to improve detection and response.
Future research should focus on clinical Zika outcomes among individuals previously exposed to dengue virus.

sentences.text: Under nitrogen deprivation, filaments of the cyanobacterium Anabaena develop a one-dimensional pattern of nitrogen-fixing heterocysts separated by about ten photosynthetic vegetative cells.

The transcription factor HetR is essential for heterocyst differentiation in Anabaena, and its gene expression fluctuations were studied using a chromosomal hetR-gfp fusion under nitrogen-rich and nitrogen-deprived conditions.
Gene expression fluctuations of hetR in nearby cells along Anabaena filaments are coupled with a spatial range of about two to three cells.
Correlations in hetR expression between cells mainly arise from intercellular molecular transfer rather than cell division.
Fluctuations after nitrogen step-down build on an underlying spatial pattern present under nitrogen-replete conditions.

Basal expression of the HetR inhibitor PatS, cell-cell communication influenced by the septal protein SepJ, and positive HetR auto-regulation determine fluctuations in hetR expression under nitrogen-rich conditions.

Comparison of hetR-gfp expression under nitrogen-rich and nitrogen-poor conditions highlights differences between the HetR inhibitors PatS and HetN, and between the septal proteins SepJ and FraC/FraD.

Proteins involved in activation, inhibition, and cell-cell communication combine with stochastic gene expression to control coupled fluctuations that give rise to a one-dimensional developmental pattern in Anabaena filaments.

sentences.text: Humans can learn and store multiple visuomotor mappings when feedback for each mapping is provided alternately, a process called dual-adaptation.
Learned context cues associated with each visuomotor mapping can be used to switch between the stored mappings without needing feedback.
However, little is known about how associative learning between contextual cues and required visuomotor mappings generalises to novel but similar conditions.

To study this, participants performed a rapid target-pointing task where visual feedback was shifted horizontally depending on the target shape, which served as a continuous contextual cue for different visuomotor mappings.
The target shapes were morphed continuously between spiky and circular forms, creating a continuous set of shapes linked to different visuomotor mappings.
After training, participants were tested without feedback on novel target shapes that had not been learned previously to assess generalisation.

The study compared two hypotheses: an explicit linear hypothesis where participants extract a linear relationship between shape and mapping, and an implicit Bayesian learning model predicting categorisation-like generalisation.

Results showed that although participants needed explicit awareness of the cue's role, they applied the mapping corresponding to the trained shape most similar to the current one, consistent with the Bayesian learning model.
The Bayesian learning model also predicted that learning slows down as the number of training pairs increases, which was confirmed by the experimental results.

Overall, the Bayesian learning model, which treats each shape-mapping pair independently using a Mixture-of-Kalman-Filters approach, provides a possible mechanism for simultaneously learning multiple visuomotor mappings.

sentences.text: Many NTD-endemic countries have not been able to launch or scale-up programs because they lack the necessary baseline data for planning and advocacy.
Because NTDs tend to overlap in geographic areas, an integrated mapping approach might result in resource savings by identifying populations needing treatment more efficiently.

We developed and field-tested an innovative integrated NTD mapping protocol called Integrated Threshold Mapping (ITM) for lymphatic filariasis, trachoma, schistosomiasis, and soil-transmitted helminths.
The ITM protocol is designed to be resource-efficient and determines whether a threshold to trigger public health interventions in an implementation unit has been reached.
The protocol uses WHO-recommended indicators in disease-specific age groups, sampling by district for most diseases but by sub-district for schistosomiasis to improve practicality.
We tested the ITM protocol by comparing it to current WHO mapping methodologies in one district each in Mali and Senegal.

The ITM methodology reached the same conclusions as WHO methods for starting public health interventions for trachoma, lymphatic filariasis, and soil-transmitted helminths, but gave more targeted intervention recommendations for schistosomiasis.
The ITM methodology was practical, feasible, and showed overall cost savings compared with the standard WHO methodologies.
This integrated mapping tool could facilitate the implementation of much-needed NTD programs in endemic countries by making mapping easier and more affordable.
